prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B019 alone, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read all six first-round statements, I find the scientific case stronger and not merely shared. Every member independently described the same chain, from proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1 peptide through human physiology and receptor biology to long-acting agonists, and every member located the weakness in attribution, not in merit or maturity. The effect on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes is confirmed in several large randomized trials, and as a neurologist and clinician I see its reach in practice. The citation I propose rests on physiology and the active peptide form, and it says that these discoveries made the therapies possible. It does not claim the drugs themselves and does not rule on the Mojsov and Habener question.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is credit. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) form is contested, Habener is outside the credited names, and none of us can settle the history from the supplied record. Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide design made the drugs practical, is left out by the three-person cap, and a physiology-centred prize will be read by some as passing over the people who reached patients. Long-term safety and durability, including pregnancy and young patients, are still accumulating. I considered a two-part prize with B030 and concluded that it would force B019 below three names and weaken a configuration whose main flaw is already attribution. I also considered whether the Habener question should push Knudsen into the third place, and I concluded that it should not, because the supplied evidence does not show that Mojsov's claim fails.

responses.point: Knudsen's drug design is arguably as decisive for patients as the physiology, so the question of crediting development is not separate, and the citation should say that the physiology enabled the therapies without claiming the drugs.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most, and I now accept that the Knudsen question is part of the case rather than a side issue. I still do not put her in the trio. With three places, the citation is most defensible when anchored in the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, and the committee cannot rank industrial design against the identification of the hormone's action without a clearer record. I adopt your wording that the physiology enabled the therapies, and I would say so explicitly. I also agree that Habener's absence is a limit of the ballot and not evidence about priority. If the Committee judged the Mojsov record to be weaker than we assume, Knudsen is the natural replacement, and a Holst and Drucker pair is a defensible fallback.

responses.point: B040 (Walter and Mori) is a clean pair and he would rank the unfolded protein response higher, and he warns that unanimity may hide differing views on basic discovery versus drug development.
responses.response: Your warning is fair, and I have tested my own view against it. My preference for B019 does not come from favouring applied work. It comes from the fact that B019 combines a basic discovery with an independently confirmed clinical result, while B040 has only the first. I agree that B040 has the cleanest attribution of the candidates beyond B019, apart from Ron and Kaufman, and I now treat it as a strong alternative, which is why I add it to my list over B012. I still hold that its disease link is mostly mechanistic and that it fits better as a later prize than as a second part sharing 2026 with B019. If B019 stood alone, B040 would be the first candidate I would raise for a coming year.

responses.point: The priority dispute is a weakness of the academic trio that the committee should state openly, and B040 is the strongest basic-science alternative but not a competitor to B019.
responses.response: I agree that stating the dispute openly is better than hiding it, and I would keep it in the committee record while leaving the citation neutral. I also agree with your framing of B040 as an alternative rather than a competitor. Where I differ is on how far this weakens B019. A contested priority for one peptide form does not remove Holst's physiology or Drucker's biology, and neither of them depends on the dispute. This is why I judge the trio robust enough, whereas an unresolved attribution for TOR, which you and I discussed, would leave the same uncertainty without comparable clinical confirmation.

responses.point: The third B019 place is a real choice between Mojsov and Knudsen, and a Holst and Drucker pair is a possible fallback.
responses.response: I agree that this is the real decision, and I would answer your question as follows. On the supplied record there is no basis for removing Mojsov, because the identification of the active peptide form is the discovery on which the later drug design depended. A Holst and Drucker pair would be cleaner but would lose that step. I would revisit if the committee saw documentary evidence that Habener's group had priority. Optogenetics, which we both rank highly, stays an alternative for a later year because of the six-name allocation problem, and I do not put it on my list of alternatives this round.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be defended against Habener's group, given that the record available to us cannot settle it.
Whether the citation can recognise the long-acting analogue step by wording alone without crediting Knudsen by name.
Whether B030 (CAR-T), with Eshhar's concept and the question of Rosenberg's role unsettled, would have a fair three-name group if it became the second choice.
Long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy remain unsettled.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. As chair I disclose my past postdoctoral work with Paul Greengard and co-authored works with committee member Thomas Perlmann on dopamine-neuron topics. Neither involves any credited name on the shortlist, and the discussion has revealed no new tie, so I see no need for recusal.
